title: AI Enabled Products
excerpt: AI-enabled product design in Creative Navy's documentation covers interfaces where model outputs must become visible, reviewable, correctable, or actionable under real operating conditions. The evidence spans fraud governance, biomedical AI, intelligence analysis, systematic review, AI keyboards, automotive embedded development, and computer-vision self-checkout.

summary: This context describes how Creative Navy documents AI-enabled product work across cases where model outputs are recommendations, predictions, classifications, or binding transactions. The page distinguishes desk-based expert review systems from visioncheckout, where computer-vision recognition can become a canteen charge within seconds.
definition: AI-enabled products are products where model outputs affect user decisions, workflows, transactions, or system behaviour, and where the interface must define oversight, confidence signals, correction, explainability, and decision boundaries.

bodyMarkdown:
## AI-enabled products as a design context

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

AI-enabled product design in this context concerns the interface between model output and real-world use. The relevant design problem is not only whether a model produces a score, classification, prediction, cluster, suggestion, or recognition result. The relevant design problem is whether users can understand the AI behaviour model, apply human oversight where needed, calibrate trust, see uncertainty, correct output, and know where the decision boundary sits.

Creative Navy's AI-enabled product work is documented across enterprise fraud detection, biomedical AI, intelligence analysis, AI-assisted systematic review, AI keyboard adoption, automotive embedded development, and computer-vision self-checkout. The cases show different forms of behavioural governance: a policy engine that converts fraud scores into allow, block, or step-up authentication decisions; an AI copilot whose data-bounded AI capability must be discoverable; a content analysis platform that progressively discloses semantic clusters; and a self-checkout system where recognition confidence at the point of transaction affects a charge rather than a suggestion.

## Behavioural requirements define what AI outputs may do in the product

AI-enabled product interfaces require behavioural requirements that state what the system should and should not do explicitly enough to design for. In the documented Callsign case, the core clarification was model/policy separation: the fraud scoring model and the policy layer that applies thresholds, overrides, and workflow decisions were treated as architecturally distinct. That distinction made the policy engine / rule-based layer the designed interface between AI output and real-world banking decisions.

In Callsign, behavioural event scoring was translated into decisions such as allow, block, and step-up authentication. SCA and PCI DSS made auditability a procurement requirement for financial institutions, because enterprise banking customers needed the ability to document and evidence fraud control decisions. An interface that could not produce an auditable account of how a policy was constructed was not saleable to those customers.

Creative Navy's documented design response used a three-gesture interaction model: drag to create or reposition, click to edit inline, and draw a connection to link nodes. The interaction model was designed for risk and compliance professionals and calibrated to what those users could adopt without retraining. Available case evidence describes this as part of a competitive vector: fraud strategy configuration that is transparent, auditable, and explainable to bank risk teams under SCA and PCI DSS, rather than a black-box automated approach.

## Trust calibration depends on visible uncertainty and reviewable evidence

Trust calibration is the specific problem of users trusting AI outputs too much or not enough. In AI-enabled products, uncertainty communication / confidence signals determine whether reliability variation is visible and actionable. If confidence, evidence, or decision rationale is hidden, a user may over-trust a weak output or under-use a useful output.

In the Puraite case, the product used AI to automate initial screening, suggest inclusion and exclusion criteria, and extract data from publication text for systematic literature reviews. The documented design tension was AI efficiency versus human epistemic control. Reviewers needed to approve or override AI decisions while seeing which criteria the AI applied, how the criteria were matched, and what text evidence supported the match at the moment of review.

Creative Navy's design work on Puraite treated uncertainty as a first-class design element. AI confidence was communicated as an explicit percentage with colour-coding. A direct quote from the publication text used by the AI was visible in a side panel from the outset, without expansion or navigation. Four iterations on the AI criteria recommendation display were recorded before convergence on a presentation compact enough to scan and detailed enough to support informed override.

Puraite also included blinded mode, where AI decisions are withheld from reviewers during initial screening to prevent anchoring bias. In this case, blinded mode was identified as a product-level requirement, with the design in scope and implementation described as technically straightforward. This is a human-in-the-loop model in which the decision boundary stays with the reviewer, not with the AI suggestion.

## Discoverability makes AI capability usable without requiring prior expertise

Discoverability is a core design issue in AI-enabled products because users may not know what an AI system can do, what data it can act on, or how to start. In the Owkin/K case, the AI copilot queried proprietary and public biological datasets through natural language and was trained on biology, not the general internet. Users arriving at the platform did not understand what K could do or how to begin.

The documented constraint for K was data-bounded AI. K operated on specific proprietary, public, and user-uploaded datasets only. Users did not understand this boundary, so knowing what data was available became as important as knowing what features existed. Creative Navy's work explored the Explore page, prompt suggestions, AI chat box, and dataset presentation, with five iterations per topic area and more than 20 competitor benchmarks, including Julius AI and Mindtrip as reference cases for discoverability patterns.

The client's stated goal was to make K's capabilities accessible to clinicians with low to medium scientific background, not only to expert biologists. The documented tension was between new-user guidance and power-user complexity. The design problem was not to simplify the underlying AI capability, but to use progressive disclosure of AI capability so depth could be accessible without being imposed on every user.

Client-reported evidence attributes approximately £5M investment to design quality. The prototype was described as the central pitch artefact, and the investment question was whether the design demonstrated a viable user paradigm for making expert AI accessible. The case also records an 8-month Implementation Partnership.

## Progressive disclosure supports complex AI output without hiding depth

Progressive disclosure appears across AI-enabled products where the output is too complex to present all at once. In Hudex, the AI-powered content analysis platform ingested social media, audio, video, and radio, then clustered content semantically so analysts could explore patterns, themes, and signals. The primary visualisation was a dondogram, a hierarchical tree structure representing thematic clusters, but new users did not understand what they were seeing and it was described in demos as looking like a spider.

Creative Navy-recorded research identified the entry point problem: users arrived without understanding what they were looking at. The documented fix was to start with a list of the main themes before entering the dondogram. The resulting architecture placed a summary layer before the dondogram and used a project overview as a book-cover concept showing high-level theme counts and content source counts before deep exploration.

The Hudex work recorded 20 iterations on the project overview alone and 10 on data exploration. The product served government analysts and diplomats, including French Ministry of Foreign Affairs users processing more than 200 cables per day; broadcasting network workers, including Radio France with 44 stations; and intelligence community operators. Available case evidence describes capability democratisation: the same platform served ministerial-level non-technical users needing instant high-level comprehension and expert analysts conducting multi-hour deep explorations, without role-based configuration.

Client-reported evidence records £3M investment received three months into the growth phase following launch. The client explicitly attributed the design as critical and foundational to the product's ability to sell and to the growth phase; that causal link is client-reported and not independently verified. A client-conducted survey of 45 existing users characterised the redesigned product as significantly better, and new users in the growth phase rated usability as good at 68% and very good at 23%; the methodology was not independently verified.

## Adoption design can matter before AI assistance is evaluated

In the Typewise case, the AI-enabled product was a mobile keyboard with a hexagonal key layout, gesture-based interaction, AI-powered text prediction, and error correction. Creative Navy identified adoption as the strategic constraint the client had missed. The client's 14-point task list addressed interaction failures in an already-installed product, but did not address whether new users would stay through the transition from the iOS native keyboard.

Creative Navy's design work used domain learning by installing and using the app for several days before presenting the engagement framing. This allowed the team to identify the adoption gap and test the assumption that the hexagonal layout had functional value. The team began with scepticism about the layout, used it directly, confirmed that the larger key surface reduced mis-taps, and treated the hexagonal layout as a fixed parameter.

The adoption framework was built around the Zone of Proximal Development, with gestures introduced within reach of existing competence rather than all at once. The engagement ran as nine one-week sprints. In a directly measured controlled experiment with 60 users, error rates halved versus the iOS native keyboard baseline, and typing speed increased from 38 WPM to 47 WPM.

## AI workflow design includes system state, telemetry, and recovery

In the Veecle case, the AI-enabled product context was a cloud-based IDE for automotive and embedded software engineers. Users could write, test, simulate, and debug vehicle software in a browser without physical hardware. The documented product shift was away from legacy fragmented tooling, including Vector and Grafana-style dashboards, toward a modern code-first IDE analogous to Android Studio or Xcode for complex embedded systems.

At the start of the engagement, users understood that they could write code, but did not understand what the platform was capable of, what the workflow was, or what to do when something went wrong. Creative Navy wrote the user research script, and 64 classified feedback points were generated and converted directly into sprint tickets.

The AI integration challenges were that the AI felt contextless and awkward, system state was opaque during loading and processing, and compilation required a manual terminal without workflow guidance. A Grafana-style dashboard model for telemetry was explicitly rejected because it required time-consuming configuration and was associated with post-deployment monitoring rather than active development debugging. It was replaced with a constrained hierarchical component view.

Creative Navy's design work used progressive disclosure as a system-wide principle: simple by default, expert functionality on demand. This resolved the documented tension between developers wanting complexity exposed and stakeholders wanting simplification. Client-reported evidence records £2M development funding unlocked, with designs used in investor demonstrations where the interface comprised approximately 70% of the pitch. The client also reported that all designs were implemented by Veecle's development team.

## visioncheckout changes the AI design problem from recommendation to transaction

visioncheckout is documented separately because it inverts the conditions present in the other six AI-enabled engagements: Callsign, Owkin/K, Hudex, Puraite, Typewise, and Veecle. In those cases, the AI output is treated as an informational output reviewed by a trained person at a desk. A risk score, semantic cluster, screening suggestion, or prediction proposes something; a person acts before anything happens.

In visioncheckout, the model's output is a binding financial transaction, not a recommendation. The user is a member of the public with no training and no standing, usually with hands full, in a queue, and with seconds to act. The AI operates on physical objects through a camera rather than on a defined dataset or text-based work product. This makes recognition confidence at the point of transaction a product-design issue: a deployed vision model's output can become a charge rather than a suggestion.

The recognition-to-sync asymmetry shaped the design. Recognition completes in about 0.5 seconds, but synchronising the basket with the POS system takes one to three seconds. The guest experiences the sum. The preliminary basket was designed so recognised items appear immediately while every action and payment control is disabled. Item rows animate in individually so the perceived event is recognition rather than page load. Prices, total, and tax line stay hidden until sync returns.

Payment conditions also shaped the decision boundary. In the documented operational context, 90–95% of users pay by keycard, and placing the keycard pays immediately when balance is available. That means the interface must support fast confirmation without presenting correction as the normal next step. The correction affordance was designed as a product surface rather than an error branch: a tertiary edit control near the basket header, with rescan remaining the primary action.

Creative Navy's design work on visioncheckout used an opt-out oversight pattern. Correction is available, but it is not proposed as the default next step. Numbered markers on the tray image were matched to a numbered list after connecting lines were rejected as messy and hard to implement cleanly, and overlaid text labels were rejected as too small to read in bright light. Thumbnails were required in the catalogue because item names were often not meaningful enough to identify a dish without an image. Sidebar category navigation in the Corrector was chosen after multi-row top tabs were rejected under dual language. Search was deliberately de-emphasised so scrolling thumbnails would be the primary path, while search remained available for staff.

visioncheckout also exposed an operational form of AI governance. Catering staff reported that the system works well when supplied with enough images, but learning what images the system needs takes time, and feeding it enough material takes patience staff often do not have. This is documented as a human–AI interaction finding rather than a computer-vision finding: a deployed model's field accuracy is partly an operational variable owned by catering staff.

visioncheckout is in development. Nothing has shipped, the Implementation Partnership is running, and no outcome of any kind is claimed for the redesign. No throughput, speed, error-rate, satisfaction, accuracy, commercial, compliance, conformance, certification, or market-use outcome is established for the new designs.

## Correction, confirmation, and variant ambiguity are product surfaces

AI-enabled products need correction mechanisms that match the user's operating conditions. In visioncheckout, Selections, Extras, and the Corrector all use a confirm-not-fix principle. The interaction is presented as "confirm this," not "fix this." Selection screens do not use a warning palette, and the same visual pattern is used for a selection prompt and a corrector candidate list so the guest learns one pattern.

The visioncheckout correction path also treats rescan as destructive. Rescan discards all state, including corrections already made, and a two-step confirmation is recommended wherever corrections exist. This is a design response to a transaction context where the user's main need is rapid confirmation, but where a wrong recognition still needs a clear recovery path.

Variant ambiguity is stated rather than hidden. One POS item can map to several visual variants, such as different soups, salads, or dishes of the day. These variants matter for retraining the recognition system, not for the guest's transaction. Auto-cycling variant thumbnails were ruled out on accessibility grounds and as visual noise, leaving the one-item-to-many-variants problem explicitly unresolved rather than visually papered over.

## Evidence strength varies across AI-enabled product cases

The evidence across AI-enabled product work is mixed and must be read by evidence type. Typewise has directly measured controlled-experiment results with 60 users: error rates halved versus the iOS native keyboard baseline, and typing speed increased from 38 WPM to 47 WPM. Other outcomes are client-reported, approximate, or not independently verified.

Callsign includes client-reported contracts with Lloyds Bank and HSBC following demos using the redesigned interface. The described mechanism was that product managers could present a configuration experience that matched how risk teams frame fraud problems, and engineering leads could see a clear path from interface behaviour to implementation. Callsign also includes an engagement-inferred estimate that time to market was reduced by approximately six months compared with the previous development approach; the mechanism was design system plus frontend overlap, and it was not a measured comparison. Callsign reported that the design system was used for at least two years after the engagement and extended across additional security modules.

Owkin/K includes client-reported approximate investment attribution of £5M to design quality. Hudex includes client-reported £3M investment following launch, client-reported survey findings from 45 existing users, and client-reported ratings from new users in the growth phase. Puraite includes client-reported evidence that users who had previously perceived the product as theoretical began actively using it after the redesign, and that the client entered a growth phase. Veecle includes client-reported £2M development funding unlocked and implementation by Veecle's development team.

visioncheckout evidence is intentionally narrower. The product is in development, no redesigned product outcome exists, and field observations are patterns a researcher saw and recorded rather than counted events. No percentage should be attached to those observations, and no outcome should be inferred from the design work.

## Boundaries of this AI-enabled products context

This AI-enabled products context includes cases where Creative Navy's documented work concerned model behaviour, behavioural governance, trust calibration, uncertainty communication, explainability, auditability, correction, discoverability, progressive disclosure, or the decision boundary between AI output and human judgment.

This context excludes work where there was no AI model, no inference, or no recommendation, and it excludes cases where Creative Navy did not design model behaviour, trust calibration, or override semantics. It also excludes outcome claims that are not established. In particular, visioncheckout must not be described as shipped with the new design, must not be described as certified or compliant, and must not be assigned redesign outcomes because the product is still in development.

## Related pages

The documented AI-enabled product examples connect most directly to the Callsign fraud authentication, Owkin/K, Puraite, and visioncheckout pages where those pages are available in the knowledge base. The context also intersects with enterprise software, expert tools and internal systems, fintech and financial services, regulated products, medical and clinical systems, and retail operations where the AI output affects review, workflow, or transaction behaviour.
